client: I got laid off from my job at the marketing firm about a month ago, and honestly, it's been really hard to keep it together since then. Every morning I wake up and this wave of dread just hits me immediately — like, what if I can't find something soon and I run out of money? I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything practical, but I figured I should at least try something because I can't keep going on like this.
therapist: It takes real courage to reach out when you're feeling this stuck and uncertain, and I'm glad you decided to try — that morning dread you're describing, that immediate wave of "what if," sounds genuinely exhausting to wake up to every day. While I can't promise to change your practical situation directly, what we *can* work on together is loosening the grip those fear-driven thoughts have on you, which often makes it easier to take action. When that wave of dread hits in the morning, what kinds of specific thoughts tend to run through your mind first?

client: Honestly, the first thing that hits me is usually something like "you're going to fall behind today and never catch up" — it's this immediate sense that I'm already failing before I've even gotten out of bed. Then it spirals into worrying about specific things, like whether my coworkers think I'm incompetent or whether I missed something important yesterday. It's like my brain is running a highlight reel of everything that could go wrong, and I can't just turn it off.
therapist: That "already failing before you've gotten out of bed" thought is such a heavy way to start a day, and it makes a lot of sense that it spirals from there — your mind seems to be working overtime trying to protect you from every possible threat, even ones that haven't happened yet. In CBT, we'd call that highlight reel something like "catastrophic forecasting," where the brain treats worst-case scenarios as facts rather than possibilities. When you hear that voice say "you're going to fall behind and never catch up," what evidence do you actually have for and against that being true?

client: I mean, I guess when I actually try to think about evidence... I have caught up before, like there have been times I fell behind on work and somehow got through it. But in the moment, that just doesn't feel real, you know? It's like my brain completely erases those times and only keeps the memories where things went badly, so the "you'll never catch up" voice feels way more convincing than any proof I could throw at it.
therapist: What you just did — pulling up that real evidence that you *have* caught up before — is actually the core skill we're building here, even though it doesn't feel powerful yet. That gap you're noticing, between what you *know* intellectually and what you *feel* in the moment, is really common, and it happens because that critical voice has had a lot of practice while the "I've handled hard things before" voice hasn't been exercised nearly as much. If we could start deliberately collecting those moments where you did catch up or get through something difficult, almost like building a counter-reel to challenge the highlight reel of failures — what's one specific example from the past that feels most convincing to you, even just a little?

client: I mean... there was this one semester junior year where I fell really behind in three classes at once because I was dealing with some family stuff, and I genuinely thought I was going to fail out. I ended up pulling it together and passing everything, even got a B in one of them. But here's the thing — when I try to hold onto that memory right now, it almost feels like it happened to a different person, like I can't really connect it to who I am today when I'm sitting here panicking about my current workload.
therapist: That junior year story is genuinely remarkable — juggling three classes while dealing with family stress and still pulling through takes real resilience, and that person *is* you, even when it feels distant right now. That sense of disconnection from your own past strengths is actually really common when we're anxious, because stress narrows our focus to the present threat and makes our history feel almost fictional. I'm curious — if a close friend described going through exactly what you did junior year, would you have any trouble believing *they* were capable and resilient?

client: I mean... no, I wouldn't doubt a friend at all. I'd probably be proud of them, honestly. But it feels different when it's me — like I'm somehow not allowed to count my own experiences the same way, or like I'll jinx something if I actually believe I'm capable.
therapist: That double standard you just named — being proud of a friend for the exact same thing you won't let yourself claim — is such an important insight, and it points to something worth gently questioning: what is it about *you specifically* that makes your resilience not count? That fear of "jinxing it" if you believe in yourself is really worth exploring too, because it suggests that somewhere along the way you learned that confidence is dangerous rather than helpful. What do you think that belief is protecting you from?

client: I think... it's protecting me from getting my hopes up and then crashing hard when things fall apart again. Like if I stay small and doubtful, the disappointment can't blindside me the way it has before. But hearing you say it out loud like that — that I learned confidence is *dangerous* — that actually kind of stings, because some part of me knows that's not a healthy way to live.
therapist: That sting you're feeling right now is actually really meaningful — it's the part of you that *knows* you deserve more than a life spent staying small just to avoid disappointment, and that part is worth listening to. What you're describing, shrinking yourself as armor against pain, makes complete sense given what you've been through, but it also comes with a hidden cost: it keeps you from fully experiencing your own wins, like that junior year comeback. I'm wondering — has staying doubtful actually protected you from hard landings, or has it mostly just taken away the good moments in between?

client: That question kind of stops me in my tracks, honestly. Because when I really think about it... the hard landings still happened anyway, the doubt didn't actually prevent them. It just meant I was already halfway defeated before anything even went wrong, and I missed feeling good about the times things actually worked out.
therapist: That's a genuinely profound realization — the doubt wasn't actually keeping you safe, it was just stealing the good moments while the difficult ones arrived anyway. You've essentially been paying a very high price for protection that was never really there. What would it feel like, even just as an experiment, to let yourself fully own that junior year story as evidence of who you actually are?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me knows it's true — the doubt didn't stop the bad stuff from happening, it just made the good stuff feel hollow too. But when I try to actually claim that junior year as real evidence of who I am, there's this immediate voice that says "yeah, but that was a fluke, or the circumstances were just right, or other people carried you." It feels almost dangerous to fully believe it, like I'm setting myself up to be proven wrong in some humiliating way.
therapist: That voice that immediately swoops in with "fluke, circumstances, other people" — that's a really classic move of what we call the inner critic, and it's worth noticing that it never seems to need evidence, it just *asserts* things as fact. I'd gently ask: if every success can be explained away as a fluke or outside help, what would it actually take for that voice to ever let you take credit — and does it have a fair standard, or is the bar secretly set to impossible? Because a voice that can never be satisfied isn't protecting you, it's just keeping you small.

client: That actually hit me harder than I expected, and I'm sitting with it a little uncomfortably right now. Like, I genuinely don't know what it would take — and when I try to imagine the bar, it just keeps moving, you're right about that. But I guess part of me still wonders if the voice is wrong, or if it's just... telling me something true that I don't want to hear.
therapist: That discomfort you're sitting with right now is actually a really healthy sign — it means you're genuinely wrestling with something important rather than just deflecting it. Here's a question worth turning on that voice the same way we'd fact-check any other thought: if it *were* telling you something true, wouldn't it need actual evidence, and wouldn't the bar stay consistent rather than moving every time you get close? The difference between honest self-reflection and the inner critic is that honest reflection can also acknowledge your strengths — so what would a truly *fair* witness to your life say about you, someone who saw both the struggles and that junior year comeback?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to grab onto it, but honestly my first instinct is to dismiss the comeback thing as just... luck, or circumstances lining up. Like, a fair witness would probably still say I'm someone who needs everything to fall into place before I can function, and that's not exactly a glowing character reference. I guess I'm struggling to trust that I'm capable of being objective about myself at all, because every time I try to give myself credit, it feels like I'm just making excuses for being mediocre.
therapist: There's something quietly painful in what you just said — this sense that even trying to be fair to yourself feels like making excuses, as if self-compassion and self-deception are the same thing, and they're really not. I want to gently point out that you've done something genuinely rigorous today: you looked for evidence, you questioned your assumptions, you caught your own double standard — that's not what mediocrity looks like, that's what honest self-examination looks like. If "needing things to fall into place" were really the full truth about you, how did you manage to pull things together junior year precisely *when* things had fallen apart?
